newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Portugal marks historic voyage's 500th anniversary.
newsitem.headline: Portugal marks historic voyage's 500th anniversary.

text.p: A proud Portugal marked on Tuesday the 500th anniversary of the start of navigator Vasco da Gama's historic voyage of discovery of the sea route from Europe to India and the Far East.

As the Portuguese never tire of reminding neighbouring Spain, it was the route to the riches of the Orient that Christopher Columbus thought he found when he reached the shores of America on behalf of the Spanish monarchy five years earlier.

Portugal's National Commission for the Commemoration of the Discoveries will mark Vasco da Gama's date with a solemn ceremony that kicks off a year of celebrations culminating in the Expo '98 World Fair to be held in Lisbon.
The fair, to run from May to September 1998, will resemble the Universal Exhibition staged in Seville, Spain, in 1992, and takes the world's oceans as its theme in homage to da Gama.
On July 8, 1497, the young Vasco da Gama, whose exact age was unknown but probably less than 30, set sail with a fleet of four ships weighing no more than 100 tonnes each.
They were assigned by King Dom Manuel I to round the southern tip of Africa and reach the exotic shores of India.

From their privileged geographical position at the southwestern corner of Europe, Portuguese adventurers had already sailed down the western coast of Africa, with Bartolomeu Dias reaching Africa's Cape of Good Hope in 1488.
Da Gama, whose mission was to find "Christians and spices", reached the Indian coast just south of Calcutta in May 1498.
His fleet, reduced to three ships by the ravages of scurvy, finally returned to Lisbon in July 1499 after what was then the longest ever recorded sea journey.
"It was a journey that changed the world," said Antonio Hespanha, chairman of the commission on the discoveries. "It brought European and Eastern civilisations into direct contact."

It also launched a golden age for Portugal which left it master of large chunks of southern Africa as well as Brazil and territories as far east as Macau on the Chinese coast and East Timor on the eastern fringe of present-day Indonesia.
Portugal retained the Indian district of Goa until 1961, 14 years after India won independence from Britain.

Its African dependencies were surrendered in the mid-1970s after a series of bloody colonial wars. Portugal's final overseas territory -- Macau -- will be formally handed over to China in December 1999.
